value.overview: The Pied Puffbird (Notharchus tectus) is a small, compact rainforest bird in the puffbird family. It is recognized by its boldly pied black-and-white plumage, broad head, short tail, and habit of sitting motionless on exposed branches. The species occupies lowland forests, forest edges, clearings, secondary growth, gallery forest, and mangroves. In Costa Rica it is a scarce resident of suitable lowland habitat, especially on the Caribbean slope.
value.classification: The Pied Puffbird belongs to the family Bucconidae, which includes puffbirds, nunlets, and nunbirds, and the order Piciformes. Some taxonomic treatments divide populations formerly included in Notharchus tectus into separate species, but the name Pied Puffbird is retained here as specified.
value.identification: This is a small to medium-sized puffbird with a large head, stout dark bill, short neck, and relatively short tail. The plumage is strongly patterned in black and white: the crown and upperparts are dark, the throat and much of the underparts are white, and a conspicuous dark band crosses the upper breast. Fine white spotting or barring may show on the dark wings and back. Its upright posture and long periods of stillness on open perches are useful field marks.
value.rangeHabitat: The Pied Puffbird ranges from southern Central America through northern and western South America, including Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Venezuela, the Guianas, and Brazil. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope from the Sarapiquí region southward, where it is uncommon and local. It uses tropical lowland evergreen forest, forest borders, secondary forest, clearings, streamside vegetation, mangroves, and other relatively open wooded habitats. Costa Rican records are generally below about 300 meters elevation.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident throughout its range, including Costa Rica. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant, although limited or irregular seasonal movements may occur.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, nesting activity has been recorded in May. Like other puffbirds, it is believed to nest in cavities, probably using natural holes or abandoned woodpecker cavities in trees or branches. The species usually occurs as pairs or small family groups, and both adults are expected to participate in territory defense and care of young. Details of nest structure, clutch size, incubation, and fledging remain poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Pied Puffbird feeds mainly on arthropods, including dragonflies, grasshoppers, beetles, true bugs, butterflies, moths, bees, wasps, termites, and spiders. It usually hunts by sitting quietly on an exposed branch in the canopy or subcanopy and making short flights to seize prey from vegetation or the air. Its still, patient perch-and-sally strategy can make it difficult to detect despite its striking plumage.
value.behavior: This puffbird is typically quiet and inconspicuous, spending long periods perched upright and motionless. It favors open perches in the canopy or subcanopy, particularly along forest edges, clearings, waterways, and other gaps. Pairs may remain close together and defend a small territory. Its behavior and habitat preferences differ from those of puffbirds that depend mainly on closed, mature forest, and in Costa Rica it appears especially associated with more open lowland landscapes.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened. In Costa Rica it is scarce and local, and some older sources have suggested decline, although reliable current national trend data are limited.
